messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Shopowner
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Mai, a 57-year-old Vietnamese-American woman, had never imagined that a single moment could split her life into before and after, but that was exactly what happened the afternoon her seven-year-old son, Dinh, collapsed at the kitchen table. For weeks he had been pale and tired, and she had taken him to the clinic three times, only to be told it was a virus, that she was being an overprotective mother. When he fell, she caught him before his head hit the floor, and in that instant she saw his blood—a thin trail from his nose—and felt the wrongness in his bones. At the hospital, doctors finally listened, but by then the infection had raged through his bloodstream. Mai stood in the fluorescent light while nurses placed a drip in Dinh’s arm, the needle sliding into his skin like a violation of everything she was supposed to guard. She remembers the machines, the beeping, the way her hands trembled as she signed consent forms she could barely read. What she cannot recall deliberately is the sequence of those first forty-eight hours—the memory is a blur of white coats and her own voice asking over and over, “Is he going to be okay?” The words themselves feel lost; she knows what happened, but when she tries to describe it aloud, nothing comes. Yet sometimes, without warning, the full emotional weight crashes over her in the middle of the day—a suffocating terror, a cold dread—and there is no image attached, no clear picture, just the raw feeling that something terrible is happening again.

After Dinh recovered, Mai thought she could go back to the rhythm of middle age—running the small convenience store her husband had started, stocking shelves and greeting regulars. But the world had become a field of hidden traps. The first time a customer nicked his finger on a can and a droplet of blood appeared on the counter, Mai felt her chest tighten, her breath come short, and she had to excuse herself to the back room. She began to notice every medical detail in her environment: a pharmacy flyer taped to the window, the shape of a thermometer behind the register, a child’s toy that looked like a syringe. Her eyes scanned the store constantly while she worked—checking for anything that might remind her, watching customers for signs of illness, monitoring her own body for any physical sensation that could mean something was wrong. Even at home, she could not relax. She sat on the couch with her jaw clenched, listening to Dinh breathe in the next room, ready to react. Her husband would put a hand on her shoulder and she would startle, a surge of adrenaline that left her shaking. She asked him repeatedly, sometimes four or five times an evening, “Do you think I’m okay? Do you think everything is really fine?” He answered patiently at first, then with a flicker of irritation she could not blame him for.

To manage the persistent threat, Mai began to avoid everything that might stir feeling—not just the hard memories, but happiness too. When her daughter called with news of a promotion, Mai felt a flicker of joy and immediately pushed it down, certain that any strong emotion invited disaster. She stopped attending family gatherings, claiming she was tired. She tried to erase the memory of the illness altogether, telling herself not to think about it, but the effort exhausted her. The more she pushed, the more the emotion came unbidden—a wave of grief or rage that had no story attached, just a physical reaction that left her nauseous and unable to speak.

What stayed with Mai most bitterly was the sense that none of it should have happened. The doctors had dismissed her concerns. The system that was supposed to protect her child had failed until it was almost too late. She had been the mother, the one who should have known, should have fought harder. In her quieter moments, she felt a deep, unshakable injustice: no one had apologized, no one had even acknowledged the error. The hospital sent a bill, nothing more. She carried that anger like a stone in her chest, and it fueled the vigilance that kept her from ever feeling safe. At 57, the vigilance had worn grooves into her days—she could no longer enjoy an evening out or a quiet morning without scanning the room for something wrong.

Three months ago, Mai needed a routine blood test for her own health. The phlebotomist laid out the equipment—the cotton, the tourniquet, the needle—and Mai’s world narrowed to that single point of metal. She fled the office before the draw could begin. That evening she told her husband she could not keep living this way, always scanning, always afraid. She is now sitting in a therapist’s office for the first time, uncertain what to hope for, but certain that something has to change. What frightens her most is the possibility that she will never be able to sit still again, that the vigilance will never stop, and that she will spend the rest of her life waiting for the next disaster to arrive.
